newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress raises pressure on government.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress raises pressure on government.

text.p: India's Congress party on Thursday ordered its lawmakers to vote against Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda in a confidence motion as the nation's 12-day-political crisis deepened.

The Congress notice to deputies increased pressure on Deve Gowda's centre-left ruling coalition to bow to its rival's demand that the prime minister relinquish power before the test vote set for Friday.

Talks between the two political formations ended in deadlock, with the United Front alliance refusing to abandon its support for Deve Gowda, who took power at the head of the minority government last June after inconclusive elections.
"We stand by our demand for change in leadership," said Tariq Anwar, political secretary to Congress president Sitaram Kesri. "The talks have failed."

If both the Congress and the rightwing opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) voted against Deve Gowda on Friday, his government would be sure to fall as it lacks an outright majority in the hung parliament.

That would force President Shankar Dayal Sharma to turn to another politician -- probably from either Congress or the BJP -- to try to form a fresh government, or the president could call the second general elections in a year.
The United Front and Congress were engaged in high-stakes brinksmanship ahead of the vote of confidence.

United Front leaders said they were unwilling to bow to Congress's demand that they force Deve Gowda to step down, while Congress said it was ready to topple the prime minister in the lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha.

"All Congress members of the Lok Sabha are requested to be present without fail, cancelling all their other engagements of whatever importance or urgency they might be on tomorrow, defeat the motion of confidence and support the party stand," the Congress whip order said.

Politicians on both sides said there remained a possibility the United Front and Congress would hold another round of talks to try to reach an agreement before the test vote, but the outlines of a compromise had not yet emerged.
Kesri, citing a drifting economy and rising communal tensions, withdrew his party's support for Deve Gowda on March 30, triggering the political crisis and raising the prospect of mid-term elections.
Kesri first said he wanted power, but has since said he would settle for Deve Gowda's resignation.
Waiting in the wings was the Hindu nationalist BJP, which emerged as the largest single party in parliament in inconclusive elections last year. With its allies, it controls 193 seats.
The 15-member United Front has 180 deputies in the 542-member lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha, while the Congress has 140 legislators.

The Lok Sabha was set to convene on Friday at 11 a.m. (0530 GMT) and was expected to debate the confidence motion before taking a vote. The prime minister would need a simple majority of those present and voting to win.
Many politicians feel President Sharma would invite the BJP to form a government if Deve Gowda lost the vote.
The BJP ruled for 12 days last May, only to quit on failing to muster a majority, paving the way for Deve Gowda to assume power.
